title: Chapter 9: Three Kinds, Three Days
blurb: Fintan sits the Chainman's Walk with ballast he made himself, and someone has slipped a letter into his folder.

blocks.text: On day eighty, at nine in the morning, the Chief Examiner broke the seal on the envelope and read the Chainman's Walk aloud to the threshold room.

"Kinds: private knot, marked stone, coined word. Route: the Bole to Copper Steps. Copper Steps to Fallowgate. Fallowgate to the Bole." She folded the paper once. "Trainee Ardent, you may open the door."
Three years in the Survey. Eighty days in the field. I had never once opened a door.
Footnote: I had rehearsed this on the coal-shed door at home. It opens onto coal.

The kinds had come three days earlier, on day seventy-seven, on a notice pinned by the Exchange Desk at the evening bell. Three kinds, no designs. The route stayed sealed until the morning, as the day-forty-two notice had promised. The hazards were not mentioned at all.
Verity Sallis was at her end of the desk, nearest the window, filling a printed grid with pencil.
"You designed the hazards," I said.
"I did."
"How many are there?"
"Forty-four percent you'll ask me that again before Thursday." She didn't look up. "Ask anyway. It improves my tables."

I didn't ask again. I had a copied pin card in my case with Nell Pardoe's hinge first on its route, and I didn't mention that either. Her pencil never slowed. I went home to Weir Lane and made ballast.

The rules are short. Ballast is made at home, in your native branch, by an act. Show it to anyone, or tell anyone, and it's spoiled. It settles at the seventh midnight after you made it and stops working. One goes per exit, the oldest valid one first. Make them too early and they're dead by the Walk.
So I timed them.
Day seventy-seven, after supper, with my bedroom door shut: a private knot, of my own design, tied into the lining of my right cuff. My left cuff held the last one, until Ferrytown took it.

Day seventy-eight: a pebble from the yard, scratched with a mark I'd never made before, and a name for it, said once and not again. My mother knocked while I was naming it. I said, "Not yet," through the wood. A voice through a shut door is not a witness. I checked.
"Edric," she said, "your tea's going cold."
It went cold.
Day seventy-nine: a coined word, said once, into a pillow, the way I'd done it for Greyfell.
Then I opened my kinds ledger, in pinned ink, and wrote three lines. Kind, day made, which goes first. Never the design. A ledger is only ink, and ink can be read.
Footnote: in order of age, the knot goes first, the stone second, the word third. If the Walk needed two exits, the word would be my spare. If it needed three, I had planned badly.
Day eighty. Nine o'clock. The Ninefold's threshold room, swept.

The Chief Examiner was Surveyor First Agnes Thorley, who had examined Walks for nineteen years and had a reputation for failing people kindly. The examiner who would accompany me was Surveyor Second Ivo Penhallow. He was there to watch, not to open. Penhallow's bill was his own business, and he'd made his ballast at home. I didn't ask what.
Brisk was leaning on the wall by the stairs, which candidates' friends are allowed to do as long as they say nothing.
"How old are you today?" I said, so that she could say something.
"Twenty-seven," said Brisk. "I've been saving it."

Gideon had issued my kit at eight: chain, chalk, a fresh Form 9 folder and a goose quill, because, he said, steel nibs were for people who trusted the Fan. He read my bill upside down while he hummed, and nodded at it, and said, "Clean as a whistle, chuck, and it'll come home that way." Then he went back to the kit room.
Standing Order 9.1: read your bill at the threshold. I opened the folder.
My Form 9, in pinned ink, written the night before:
My given name is Edric. Shorthand at ninety words a minute. My father is Tobin Ardent. I remember my father's voice.

Behind the bill was a typed sheet headed TASKS, and behind that an envelope. Good paper, sealed in the Survey's red, addressed To the Chief Examiner, Ninefold Hall, by hand of the candidate. In the top right corner, a penny stamp of the Tessary Post, cancelled.
Task one: survey the Copper Steps door to Fallowgate and certify it unchanged against the card. Task two: deliver the enclosed to the Chief Examiner at the end of the Walk.
Footnote: a letter carried by hand does not need a stamp. I should have asked why it had one. I didn't, at nine o'clock. I was thinking about doors.
Thorley read the envelope. Then she said it. "Trainee Ardent, you may open the door."

Standing Order 4.2 says a trainee may not open doors. The Walk suspends it for one day, by its own rules, and only for the candidate. I had read that paragraph perhaps forty times, and the rest of the Walk rules with it: no glare lists in the candidate's folder; rule four, the candidate may consult any source in the branch. I still felt the Order's absence like a missing tooth.
The door to Copper Steps is the first on the east wall, two along from Weirside's. Plain oak, black iron, a sill worn into a shallow dish by five hundred years of boots.
I stood in it. I read the route.
"Dunmore's steps, coppered."
The door opened. Copper Steps' threshold room was on the other side, very like ours, with the morning coming in at a different slant.
"Nine," I said. "Eight. Seven."
Brisk didn't say anything. I heard her not saying it.
On six I stepped through. On five, Penhallow. On one, the door shut behind us, and the Bole's opening to Copper Steps was spent for the day.

Copper Steps is distance one. Sixty years ago Harbourmaster Dunmore had the river stairs sheathed in copper; ours chose stone. It's one hinge, and you can see all of it from the Hall's front window. The steps down to the water are green, and the whole of the waterfront smells faintly of pennies.

Task one took me forty minutes. The Copper Steps door to Fallowgate is the low one under their Hall's gallery stair: thirty-six and a half inches by seventy-four, a mason's mark like a key with three wards, low on the right jamb. I measured it twice, drew the mark, and compared both with the card. Unchanged. I signed the certificate "Ardent, Tr." and Penhallow countersigned it without a word.
Then I stood in the second door I had ever opened and read Copper Steps' side of the next pair.
"Trask's field, left fallow."
Nine. Eight. Seven. Through on six.
That reading spent Copper Steps' opening to Fallowgate. And stepping out of Copper Steps charged me my first exit of the Walk, at the door under the stair.
I read my bill in Fallowgate's threshold room with my back to the wall. Every line read true. In my right cuff, where the knot had been, the lining was smooth.
Footnote: somewhere in Copper Steps, a man with my face now has a knot in his cuff he didn't tie. It cost him nothing. That's the whole point of ballast, and I checked the rule twice anyway.

Fallowgate is distance two. In Copper Steps, forty years ago, a farmer called Trask ploughed the field by the north gate. In Fallowgate he didn't, and the town grew round the empty field instead of over it, and the gate kept the field's name.
It was a pleasant threshold room. I didn't enjoy it.
No glare lists in the candidate's folder: I'd been carrying that rule all morning without looking at it. Fallowgate's list is in a drawer in the Bole. You are meant to know your branches or find out.

Glare beats ballast. If anything I carried depended on something Fallowgate doesn't have, that thing would go at the door instead of my marked stone, and my counterpart would get it: a Bole object, impossible here, planted in a stranger's life.
And decoys are licensed from Surveyor Second, not before. A trainee who drops one on his counterpart has used a decoy without a licence. That isn't a hazard. That's a fail.
I went through what I had, which is the job.

My kit was chain, chalk, a goose quill, pinned ink, a Form 9, a task sheet, a certificate and one letter, and the clothes and boots I stood in. Fallowgate split from Copper Steps forty years ago, so anything in that kit younger than forty years might not exist here. I didn't know which of those was younger than forty years. Guessing isn't surveying.
So I went to find out.
Fallowgate's Survey keeps an Exchange Desk like ours, and the man on it that morning had my face.

Not nearly my face. My face. The same jaw, the same way of holding a pen too high up the barrel. He had ink to the second knuckle and a Chainman's tab on his collar, and he stood up when he saw me, the way you would if a mirror walked in.
"You're the Bole's," he said. "They wrote that you'd be through today. I was told not to help."
"Were you told not to answer?"
He thought about it. "No."
"Rule four of the Walk," I said. "The candidate may consult any source in the branch."
Penhallow, behind me, wrote something down. I took a broad view of "source". So, it turned out, did Penhallow.
"What's your name?" I said, because it was rude not to.
"Fintan Ardent."
He said it plainly, and it was a word, and it meant nothing to me. I wrote it down on the back of my task sheet so that I'd have it.

Footnote: here, his name is still the one I was born with. An unballasted exit from Fallowgate would take "Edric" as my oldest orphan and give me his. The arithmetic for Option 3 is clean here. I didn't run it.
"What doesn't Fallowgate have?" I said. "That the Bole does. Things younger than forty years."
He laughed, which I'd have done too.
"Plenty. We've no subscription library. No lifeboat on the estuary." He counted on inky fingers. "No Post."
"No Post."
"No Tessary Post. Nobody ever founded it. Carriers take letters, by the street, and you pay at the door." He tilted his head at me, my own head, tilted. "Why? What are you carrying?"
I took the envelope out of my folder. Red Survey seal. Penny stamp, cancelled. To the Chief Examiner, by hand of the candidate.

A stamp is the Post's. In a branch without a Post, a stamp is a thing nothing supports. Glare, by the book. It would go at the door instead of my stone, and Fallowgate's Fintan Ardent would find a letter to an examiner he'd never heard of, from a postal service his world never had.
Footnote: an hour earlier, I had wondered why a letter carried by hand needed a stamp. I'd like the record to show that I wondered.
"Thank you," I said to him.
"Is that the hazard?"
"I think so."
"Good luck, then." He sat down. "Tell your desk ours says hello."
I owed him more than that. I didn't know how to pay it, so I wrote his name a second time, under the first, and he watched me do it and didn't ask why.
Fallowgate's door to the Bole is the north-west door of their Ninefold, and it opens onto the north-west door of ours. I stood in it with the letter in my left hand and my bill in my right.
Penhallow stood behind me. He didn't ask what I was going to do. I have since found out that examiners aren't allowed to, and I respect it.
"Trask's field, ploughed," I read. "Dunmore's steps, stone."
The door opened. On the far side, in the Bole's threshold room, the Chief Examiner was standing two paces off the sill, exactly where an examiner stands.
"Nine," I said.

I reached through the open door with the letter. My hand was in the Bole and the rest of me was in Fallowgate. Reaching through isn't a crossing. Hand-passed objects cross freely. It costs nothing at all.
"Eight. By hand of the candidate, Examiner."
Thorley took it.
"Seven." I stepped through.
On five, Penhallow. On two, the north-west door shut, and Fallowgate's opening to the Bole was spent for the day.
I read my bill standing on the sill, as 9.1 requires.
My given name is Edric. True. Shorthand at ninety words a minute. True. My father is Tobin Ardent. True. I remember my father's voice. True.

My left trouser pocket, where the scratched pebble had been, was empty. The marked stone had gone at Fallowgate's door, as the oldest ballast I still had. Nothing glared, because nothing I carried through could. The letter was already home.
Thorley slit the envelope with her thumb. Inside was a single card, in Verity's handwriting: If you are reading this in the Bole, the candidate passed hazard one.
"There was only one," said Thorley. "Sallis argued for three. I argued for one done properly." She held out her hand. "Chainman Ardent."

She wrote the result on the Walk sheet in pinned ink, signed it, and had Penhallow sign it. A rank is a word. A licence is a word with an exam on file in ink that doesn't change. I watched the ink dry.
Verity was by the stairs, next to Brisk. I hadn't seen her come in.
"Seventy-nine percent you'd miss it," she said.
"You put a stamp on a hand-carried letter."
"Nobody looks at stamps." She considered me. "You asked your counterpart."
"I did."
"That wasn't in my tables." She made a note. "It will be."

Swap bill for day eighty: two exits, two ballasts. Knot at Copper Steps, stone at Fallowgate. My coined word unspent; it will settle on its own and nobody will ever know it. Three openings, one per pair: the Bole's to Copper Steps, read by me; Copper Steps' to Fallowgate, read by me; Fallowgate's to the Bole, read by me.
Footnote: three doors. Brisk says I count the breaths like a pilot now. I have decided to take that as a second licence.
The Hall register is a ledger in the Cartographer's room, bound in green leather, written in pinned ink, and nobody but a Cartographer may make an entry in it. Cressida made mine at four o'clock.
Ardent, E. Chainman. Day eighty. Walk on file.
She blotted it and closed the book and didn't tell me to go. So I stayed. She took her time over the pen.
"You asked me on day fifty-one where ballast came from," she said. "You haven't asked since."
"No, Cartographer."
"Why?"
"You stopped answering."
"And now you're licensed." She put the pen in the tray, square. "A Chainman crosses alone. He should know what he's carrying."
I waited. It's the only thing that works with her.

"Forty crossings," she said. "You've read my books. After the fortieth I stopped. Eleven weeks. I'd lost forty things and couldn't name one. I didn't know what I was missing. I only knew there was a lot of it."
"The idle weeks."

"In those weeks a traveller from the far end found me. In a week, he taught me all thirty-one kinds. Every one. He told me there were no others." She tapped the Ballast Book on the corner of her desk, the copy with the cracked spine. "Page one is his sentence. In my handwriting."
I didn't say anything. There was a good deal I could have said, and none of it was a question she'd answer.
"He never asked me to call it mine," said Cressida. "That part was mine."
"What was his name?"

"I don't have his name. I don't have his branch. I have an old man's face I've never once been able to place." She looked at the register, not at me. "The far end. That's what I have. Thirty-one years, Ardent, and that's what I have."
Footnote: I had the page number, the week, and the handwriting. I didn't have him. Neither, I realised, did she.
"There's an order I give every new Chainman," she said. "I've never once followed it myself. When someone knows more than they should, ask their name. Write it down."
"Yes, Cartographer."
"Not 'yes'. Write it down."
I opened my Form 9 folder and wrote it under the bill, in pinned ink, in her words, and she watched me do it until the last full stop.
"Good," she said. "Go away."
I went.
Late that afternoon I found Verity at her end of the Exchange Desk, still filling in her grid, and asked her to come to the Far Map drawers with me.
"I have something you should see," I said, "and I should have shown somebody three weeks ago."

I'd had it in my case since day fifty-nine: the plain card from under the bench by the Chapter door. Gannet Light, distance ten, in our notation, in our route order, with our hinge-maker field filled in, copied in ordinary ink from a card in these drawers.

She read it once. She read the first hinge on the route: Pardoe's coast, yes. Nell Pardoe's. Somebody had copied a child's decision out of our drawers and carried it about. She went the colour she'd gone on day fifty-eight.
"Why didn't you show someone?"

"It was copied in our notation, from our drawers. I didn't know who to hand it to." I put it on the table. "That's the only thing I know about whoever made it. So I want to know what else in these drawers doesn't add up."

We took the board first. Every red pin from the first of last year to tonight. Six from last year. Sixteen from this. Twenty-two. Lowbridge, Ashcombe, Brackwater, Brindle Reach, Wrencote, and seventeen I knew only as names. This time I counted.
Then we pulled the twenty-two cards and laid them out on the long table and looked for what they had in common.

Not distance: twenty to thirty-eight. Not age: Wrencote was pinned fifty-three years ago; one of them, eleven. Not the door: five different Ninefold doors. Not the crew who'd pinned them, or the side of any one hinge, or the season.
Verity found it a little before the evening bell, because she was the one with the grid.
"Hinge-maker," she said.

Every far card is meant to name the person who made the branch's hinge. Not every card manages it. Finding a hinge is archive work. You can read a route for decades before anybody works out whose decision it was; Weirside's own card was provisional for twenty-one years. So a far card can be live and true and still have a blank in the hinge-maker field.
I counted those as well. Cards at distance twenty and beyond, living and dead: a hundred and fifty. With a hinge-maker named: a hundred and four. Still provisional, field empty: forty-six.

Twenty-two dead in two years. Every one of them from the hundred and four. Lowbridge, with a name in the field. Brackwater: Absalom Reay, copied from Greyfell's card. Wrencote: Tamsin Rooke, mill-owner. Not one dead pin from the forty-six that nobody has a name for.
Verity did the sum twice, the second time slowly.

"If the field had nothing to do with it," she said, "you'd see this about once in six thousand eight hundred tries. Nought point nought one five percent, Ardent." She put the pencil down and didn't snap it. "So it has something to do with it."
"What?"
"I don't know." She said it as if it cost her something. "Neither do you."
I looked at the copied card, and then at the twenty-two laid out beside it. A name in a field on a card. A branch alive or dead. I couldn't find one thing that joined the two.
Noted.
Footnote: that is a correlation, not a cause. I wrote it down that way: a correlation, a copy, a count. I didn't write down a reason. I didn't have one to write.
At the evening bell I went down to the Exchange Desk to post a line to my mother. Chainman, I was going to write. Home late.
Miss Tolliver was sealing the Weirside packet. She looked up and took a letter out of my pigeonhole.
"Held for you since the dawn packet, Chainman."
Green wax. Weirside's Survey uses no other.

A Chainman may open any door to distance two, and cross it alone. I knew four such routes by heart, two of them since this morning. The first I ever learned, the one I'd been saying under my breath for eighty days, was Weirside's.
I broke the seal. Four short lines, in my own handwriting, signed only Ardent.
Come now. Come alone. Bring ballast.
